vulnerability_analysis: The contract has two low-level calls without return value checks in swapBack() and withdrawStuckETH(). This allows an attacker (who is the owner) to drain ETH from the contract by setting operationsAddress to a malicious contract that selfdestructs with the attacker as beneficiary. When swapBack() is called, it sends ETH to operationsAddress via a low-level call. The malicious contract's receive() function executes selfdestruct(attacker), forcing ETH to the attacker, then the call appears to fail (but success is not checked). The contract continues execution thinking the transfer failed, but the ETH is already with the attacker.
attack_strategy: 1. Deploy a malicious contract with a receive() function that selfdestructs to the attacker. 2. As owner, set operationsAddress to the malicious contract. 3. Transfer tokens to the contract to increase its token balance above swapTokensAtAmount. 4. Call forceSwapBack() which will swap tokens for ETH and attempt to send ETH to operationsAddress. 5. The malicious contract selfdestructs, sending ETH to attacker. 6. The low-level call doesn't check success, so the operation completes.
step_by_step_plan: 1. In setUp(), impersonate the owner of the target contract. 2. Deploy a SelfDestructContract that selfdestructs to the attacker address. 3. Call setOperationsAddress() on the target contract to point to the SelfDestructContract. 4. Transfer some tokens from owner to the target contract (since owner has all initial supply). 5. Call forceSwapBack() on the target contract. 6. The SelfDestructContract will receive ETH and selfdestruct to attacker. 7. Verify attacker's ETH balance increased.
